passage: A simple pendulum is a small, heavy bob hanging from a light string. The period of a pendulum is the time it takes the bob to swing from one side to the other and back again. Students built pendulums from a 200 g brass bob and strings of five different lengths, measured from the pivot to the center of the bob. For each length, they pulled the bob aside until the string made a given angle with the vertical (the release angle), released it, and timed 20 complete swings with a stopwatch. They divided each time by 20 to find the period. Each length was tested at a release angle of 10° and at a release angle of 40°. The 200 g bob was used in every trial. Table 1 shows the results.

prompt: Suppose the students wanted to find out whether the mass of the bob affects the period of a pendulum. Which of the following sets of trials would best test this?
choices: Bobs of 100 g, 200 g, and 400 g, each on a 1.00 m string released at 10°
A 200 g bob on strings of 0.50 m, 1.00 m, and 2.00 m, each released at 10°
Bobs of 100 g, 200 g, and 400 g on strings of 0.50 m, 1.00 m, and 2.00 m, respectively
A 200 g bob on a 1.00 m string released at angles of 10°, 20°, and 40°
correct_answer: Bobs of 100 g, 200 g, and 400 g, each on a 1.00 m string released at 10°

passage:
In an iodine clock reaction, hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) reacts with iodide ions (I⁻) from potassium iodide (KI) to produce iodine (I₂). The reaction mixture also contains starch and a small, fixed amount of sodium thiosulfate. Thiosulfate immediately converts any iodine back to iodide, so no iodine builds up until all the thiosulfate is used. At that moment, iodine combines with starch and the mixture suddenly turns blue-black. The shorter the time until the color change, the faster the reaction.

In every trial, 25 mL of a KI solution containing starch and 0.0010 mol of sodium thiosulfate was mixed with 25 mL of an acidified 0.50 M H₂O₂ solution, and the time until the color change was recorded. Unless stated otherwise, the KI concentration was 0.10 M, both solutions were at 20 °C, and no catalyst was added.

Experiment 1
The KI concentration was varied.

Experiment 2
Both solutions were brought to the same temperature before mixing, and the temperature was varied.

Experiment 3
Drops of an ammonium molybdate solution, which acts as a catalyst for this reaction, were added to the KI solution before mixing. The number of drops was varied.

The results are shown in Table 1.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Time to color change in Experiments 1-3

prompt: According to the results of Experiment 2, what was the time to color change at 30 °C?
explanation: In Table 1, Trial 7 (Exp. 2, 30 °C) has a time of "31 s." The times 16 s, 60 s, and 118 s are the Experiment 2 results at 40 °C, 20 °C, and 10 °C.

In autumn, the leaves of many deciduous trees change color before they fall. Yellow and orange colors come from carotenoid pigments that are present in the leaf all summer and become visible as the green pigment chlorophyll breaks down. Red colors are different: they come from anthocyanin pigments, which most of these trees make new in autumn, in the last weeks before the leaves drop. During those same weeks, the tree moves nitrogen and other nutrients out of the dying leaves and into its branches and roots, where they are stored for the next spring. Two hypotheses explain why trees make red pigment in leaves they are about to lose.

Hypothesis 1
Anthocyanins act as a sunscreen. As chlorophyll breaks down, the leaf's remaining light-capturing machinery is easily damaged by strong sunlight, especially on cold, bright days. Damaged leaves die early, before the tree has finished moving nutrients out of them. A layer of red pigment absorbs some of the incoming light and protects the leaf, so the leaf stays alive longer and the tree recovers more of its nitrogen. Leaves receiving the most sunlight need the most protection and should become the reddest. Making anthocyanins uses energy, which the tree spends only because the benefit is greater.

Hypothesis 2
Red color is a warning signal to aphids. Many aphid species fly to trees in autumn and lay eggs on them; the young that hatch in spring feed on the tree. A tree with strong chemical defenses can afford to spend energy on making anthocyanins, so an intensely red tree is advertising, as a whole, that it is well defended. Aphids that avoid red trees and lay their eggs on yellow trees leave more surviving offspring. The signal is honest because it is costly: making anthocyanins uses energy that only a vigorous, well-defended tree can spare.

making carotenoid pigments visible so that the leaves turn yellow before they fall.
correct_answer: protecting leaves from strong sunlight so that more nutrients can be recovered from them.
explanation: Hypothesis 1 says the red layer absorbs light and protects the leaf, "so the leaf stays alive longer and the tree recovers more of its nitrogen." passage_title: Heat Source of a Hot Spring
passage:
A hot spring flows from the ground where a large fault (a fracture along which rocks have moved) reaches the surface in a hilly region. The spring water is 68 °C, and its temperature has stayed within 1 °C of that value for the 120 years it has been recorded. The average yearly air temperature in the region is 12 °C. The youngest volcanic rocks within 100 km of the spring are about 30 million years old. In most of Earth's continental crust, temperature increases with depth by about 25 °C per kilometer. Two scientists explain the source of the spring's heat.

Scientist 1
The spring is heated only by the normal increase of temperature with depth. Rain and snowmelt soak into the ground in the surrounding hills and seep downward through cracked rock along the fault. The water descends until it is warmed to the temperature of the deep rock, then rises quickly back up the fault, losing little heat on the way. Away from the fault, the temperature of the rock increases with depth at the normal rate. Because the water comes from the atmosphere and has touched only crustal rock, the helium dissolved in it should have the low ratio of helium-3 to helium-4 found in crustal rocks.

Scientist 2
The spring is heated by a body of magma, about 6 km below the surface, that has not yet solidified. Groundwater is heated by the hot rock above the magma and rises to the surface along the fault. Heat from the magma has warmed the crust throughout the area, so the temperature of the rock increases with depth far faster than 25 °C per kilometer, even away from the fault. Magma carries helium from Earth's mantle, which has a ratio of helium-3 to helium-4 about 100 times higher than that of crustal rocks, so the spring water should contain helium with an elevated ratio.

passage_title: Heat Source of a Hot Spring
passage:
A hot spring flows from the ground where a large fault (a fracture along which rocks have moved) reaches the surface in a hilly region. The spring water is 68 °C, and its temperature has stayed within 1 °C of that value for the 120 years it has been recorded. The average yearly air temperature in the region is 12 °C. The youngest volcanic rocks within 100 km of the spring are about 30 million years old. In most of Earth's continental crust, temperature increases with depth by about 25 °C per kilometer. Two scientists explain the source of the spring's heat.

Scientist 1
The spring is heated only by the normal increase of temperature with depth. Rain and snowmelt soak into the ground in the surrounding hills and seep downward through cracked rock along the fault. The water descends until it is warmed to the temperature of the deep rock, then rises quickly back up the fault, losing little heat on the way. Away from the fault, the temperature of the rock increases with depth at the normal rate. Because the water comes from the atmosphere and has touched only crustal rock, the helium dissolved in it should have the low ratio of helium-3 to helium-4 found in crustal rocks.

Scientist 2
The spring is heated by a body of magma, about 6 km below the surface, that has not yet solidified. Groundwater is heated by the hot rock above the magma and rises to the surface along the fault. Heat from the magma has warmed the crust throughout the area, so the temperature of the rock increases with depth far faster than 25 °C per kilometer, even away from the fault. Magma carries helium from Earth's mantle, which has a ratio of helium-3 to helium-4 about 100 times higher than that of crustal rocks, so the spring water should contain helium with an elevated ratio.
prompt: Based on the passage, how deep would the water have to descend for Scientist 1's explanation to account for the spring's temperature?
choices: About 0.5 km
About 2.2 km
About 2.7 km
About 5.6 km
correct_answer: About 2.2 km
explanation: The water must warm from the region's surface temperature of 12 °C to 68 °C, a rise of 56 °C. At the normal rate of 25 °C per kilometer, that requires 56 ÷ 25 = 2.24 km, "About 2.2 km." Dividing 68 by 25 ignores the 12 °C starting temperature and gives 2.7 km; 5.6 km results from using 10 °C per kilometer; and 0.5 km is far too shallow to reach 68 °C at the normal rate.
